content.summary_of_the_paper: Given a set of pairwise, possible non-transitive comparisons, this paper proposes a method to rank pairs of items that were previously not compared. The method involves learning an embedding for each item in a training dataset containing pairwise comparisons such that if $a$ is higher ranked than $b$, then the $L_\infty$ norm of the difference between their embeddings is high. Then, when given a pair of items that were previously not compared, the proposed method uses the $L_\infty$ norm of the difference between their embeddings to predict which of the items is ranked higher. The proposed method is shown to outperform two baselines on several synthetic and real world benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

- The paper is clear and well written.
- Related work is discussed comprehensively.
- The proposed method is backed by theoretical results.
- The synthetic evaluation is thorough, and illuminates various aspects of the proposed method.

Weaknesses

1. The motivation to use the $L_\infty$ norm is not discussed. Why not use all coordinates of the embeddings such as in order embeddings by (Vendrov et al, 2015), instead of just one coordinate? Why not use the majority vote of coordinates as suggested by (Makhijani and Ugander, 2019)?

2. The results in Section 7.4 are not discussed or interpreted at all. Since the results are only empirical and on a few datasets, this discussion is important to understand the generalizability and limitations of the proposed method on real world data. Why does the proposed method do well, and when might it fail? Why were these specific datasets chosen (especially the ones that are not really ranking datasets)? What happened on the one dataset where the proposed method did not outperform baselines?

3. The paper only compares with one reasonable baseline (SF-MLE), despite citing several others in the related work. For example: (Chen and Joachims, 2016), 

References

Vendrov, Ivan, Ryan Kiros, Sanja Fidler, and Raquel Urtasun. "Order-embeddings of images and language." arXiv preprint arXiv:1511.06361 (2015).

Makhijani, Rahul, and Johan Ugander. "Parametric models for intransitivity in pairwise rankings." In The World Wide Web Conference, pp. 3056-3062. 2019.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Concerns/Typos/Grammar:**

- The first paragraph of the introduction would benefit from references.
- Reference [10] in the related work appears as a sentence by itself.
- References are not numbered in the bibliography, but are numbered when cited.
- In the related work section on intransitive preferences, [4,10] are cited which assume transitive preferences.
- "alongwith"
- Section 7.4 cites Table 7.4, which does not exist.
- "two step procedure if followed"
- The argument to $\phi$ in Section 6 is just the $L_\infty$ norm of the embedding difference. This might help shorten the section and make it more precise.
- In Section 6, is the loss function the cross-entropy loss? Is there any regularization applied? There are very few details in this section, which will affect reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a simple method with some theoretical results and empirical performance gains. However, the motivation for the proposed method is unclear, comparisons against prior work is complete, and the results on real-world datasets are not discussed and interpreted.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors introduce a model for pairwise comparisons of items that models an underlying assumption that the outcome depend on the most distinguishing feature of the two items. This tries to capture some human behavior that the authors claim without relevant citations.

The authors show some properties on the types of tournaments that can and cannot appear under their model. This showcases that their model captures intrasitive preferences by showing that it can lead into cycles in the tournament.

Finally the authors evaluate their method compared to some basic baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* The problem is relevant to ICLR.

Weaknesses:
* The paper is not self-contained, is missing important references, and only compares to naive baselines in the experiments.
* Unclear setup and evaluation in the experimental section.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is of low quality, it is not self-contained, is missing many references, and the description is unclear.


== General == 


While the authors sell their model for capturing intransitive comparisons, they only show some basic properties, but never evaluate the model itself. The model is only evaluated in combination on a learned set of embeddings and it is not clear what is the role of the learned embedding and what is the effect of the comparison model as these are not evaluated separately.


== On relate work ==


The most relevant references in the section "Prior work on Intransitive Preference Modelling" is missing (and in fact has a different citation style). In fact this section seems mostly copy-pasted from Section 2 of the relevant published paper (which is not cited):
* On The Structure of Parametric Tournaments with Application to Ranking from Pairwise Comparison. Vishnu Veerathu, Arun Rajkumar. NeurIPS 2021.
This paper also considers the same problems. Given the near-identical text in the related work, I assume the authors are aware of this work.


Please include references for the Copeland score, Siamese network training, Salient Features model.


The authors claim in the introduction that they "also explore the representation power of the DF model by mapping it to a edge colouring problem on tournaments and derive several interesting sufficient conditions on the coloring that ensures representability." but I didn't get where that is in the paper.


=== On Experiments: ===


The authors do not describe how they are choosing the training set, but only reference the size of the training set. My understanding is that the Rank Centrality requires a selection of examples to allow producing scores for each pair.


It is unclear how one obtains the ground truth data of the different synthetic dataset:
* "For the BTL model, the ground truth ranking is obtained by sorting the true scores in descending order". How do you get a ranking from sorting n^2 comparisons?
* "For the SF model, the ground truth ranking is obtained by sorting the scores where the score of item i is the w T fi where w is the weight vector and fi is the feature vector corresponding to item i.". Why is this considered the ground truth?


Why do you use the Copeland method to rank the items only for your own method, and not for all methods?  


I don't think that the argument "When the underlying model is the SF-Model, the SF-MLE algorithm has an unfair advantage as it uses the features (embeddings) whereas both RC and DF-learn are not privy to the features" holds. Why don't you apply directly the DF compute model on the input data? 


The real world datasets are not cited. Also the authors do not describe what is the set of one-hot embedding or features used for applying the algorithms.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is of low quality and is not ready for publication. The related section is stolen from another paper, and the authors didn't bother to fix the citation style in that section. Also the experimental evaluation is not well described and seems biased. I recommend rejection.

content.summary_of_the_paper: An new algorithm (the Distinguishing Feature or DF model) is presented for pairwise comparison and ranking of items in settings such as recommender systems and modeling of competitive 2-entity games. Latent features (embeddings) of items are discovered by fitting to pairwise comparison preference training data in a procedure with some similarities to matrix factorization. However, the prediction is generated based on the single latent dimension which differs the most in absolute value between the latent feature vectors of the 2 items, rather than using a dot product as matrix factorization does. This "distinguishing feature" aspect of the model allows the model to generate intransitive predictions a.k.a. predictions with cycles, in which item A may be preferred to item B and item B to item C but item C is preferred to item A. Theoretical results are derived showing that an embedding dimension of 3 is sufficient to generate prediction cycles. However, certain types of preference patterns are shown to be impossible to implement with an embedding dimension of 3. A discretized evaluation metric is employed in which the model is evaluated as correct if the model's predicted probability of item i being preferred to j is above 0.5 when the actual probability is above 0.5 , irrespective of the specific values of the actual and predicted probability.  Favorable experimental results on synthetic data as well as on real-world recommendation system benchmark datasets and online video game matchup datasets are presented.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The DF algorithm is novel to the best of my knowledge. 

The ability to generate cyclic/nontransitive predictions is very interesting and is likely to have some value in settings like modeling of competitive environments such as the online video game matchup data used in the paper as well as in modeling of team and individual sports (basketball, tennis, etc) where game outcome predictions intuitively should not necessarily be transitive.

The theoretical results on d=3 being sufficient to generate some but not all cycles seem sound and are interesting results.

However, I would like to see more explanation for the need to use non-transitive modeling in a recommendation system context such as Jester and MovieLens. I understand that empirically, we may see non-transitive ratings/comparisons in real world datasets. However, that does not mean that it's necessarily beneficial to implement a model which can generate non-transitive predictions. It seems quite possible that the non-transitive data observed is better treated as noise, which would necessarily be the case if the model is transitive by design. Therefore, I would have preferred to see more benchmarking vs. a wider list of traditional, transitive models in addition to Rank Centrality, such as traditional recommendation system methods like matrix factorization. Are we sure that some of those wouldn't beat DF even though they can't model cycles?

I also find the evaluation metrics in equations 1 and 2 on page 3 to be unwisely thresholding at 0.5.  For instance, in equation 2, I would have thought a cross-entropy/log likelihood-type metric would be more appropriate. Equation 2 doesn't care if P_hat_ij is 0.99 or 0.51...as long as P_ij is above 0.5, the evaluation is the same, which doesn't seem right to me.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The reproducibility looks good, given the code in the supplemental.

The method seems to be novel.

The clarity and quality are fairly good but not as good as I would like because the motivation for using transitive models in a recommendation system is not as well justified as it should be.  As mentioned, I would like to see more evidence for recommendation systems that modeling cycles actually produces better pairwise predictions.

Another way to motivate the paper better would be to focus more on modeling of competitive situations like the video game outcomes, such as professional sports, rather than the Jester/MovieLens stuff where it's less clear whether transitivity is valuable.

I also am concerned regarding both quality and clarity about the evaluation metrics which threshold the Ps at 0.5 and otherwise ignore whether they are (for instance) 0.99 or 0.51. rather than a more intuitive and principled cross-entropy-style metric.

Here is a list of typo-ish suggested edits:

It’s prediction –> its prediction
Page 2 
Of it’s -> of its
Very few number of comparisons -> very few comparisons
Page 3
Proability -> probability

A two step procedure if followed -> A two step procedure is followed
Page 5
With only 3 dimension -> with only 3 dimensions
Page 7
For each of the model -> For each of the models
we use in the pairwise prediction -> we use is the pairwise prediction 
Page 8
 the number items -> the number of items
Page 9
Realworld -> real world  
Comaprisons-> comparisons

Table 7.4 is actually Table 1
content.summary_of_the_review: A model for generating pairwise predictions which are potentially cyclic (non-transitive) is presented. Some interesting theoretical results and somewhat encouraging experimental results are presented. However, the need for non-transitive modeling in a recommendation system context needs to be better demonstrated with more experimental benchmarking and the evaluation metric is unnecessarily discretized and throws away information about how closely the predicted and actual P_ij's agree.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers learning to rank from pairwise comparisons. The paper focuses on the intransitivity problem behind pairwise relations and proposes a distinguishing feature model to address the problem. The paper shows theoretical analysis to characterize the proposed model and experimental results on synthetic and real datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- The current submission is quite unclear, mainly in the experimental part.
- Theoretical analysis and experimental results are relatively weak to ensure the effectiveness of the proposed method compared to existing studies.
- The proposed method seems novel, but the technical contribution seems insufficient.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and Reproducibility

The detail of the experiments is somewhat unclear. The information on the model architecture (e.g., the size of each hidden layer) and the training algorithm is missing for the DF model. The computational resources and implementation details are also not mentioned. It would not be easy to reproduce the experimental results from the current submission.

Quality

The current contents are somewhat weak to support the effectiveness of the proposed method. First, the comparison to existing studies would not be enough. As shown in Section 2, other studies considering intransitivity have been presented. However, the paper did not provide theoretical or experimental comparisons to them except for 'the context dependent salient feature model.' While the experiments only compared RC and SF-MLE, there seem to be other compared methods, as in a recent study (He et al., 2022). Moreover, it appears that the DF model does not recover data with sufficient accuracy in Figures 3 and 4. For example, Figure 3 shows that only 75-78% of accuracies are recovered even for the dataset generated from the DF model with 4000 pairs.

There seems to be room to improve the presentation in the current submission. In the third paragraph of Section 2, the paper suddenly changes the citation style to the number citation. Such a presentation is inconsistent and confusing. The paper mentions the BTL model, the Thurstone model, and their computational complexities but does not cite relevant studies. I recommend citing the corresponding references to be self-contained. There appear to be several other minor errors. Those I found are listed in Minor comments and questions below.

I wonder if the paper properly presents the theoretical results in Section 5. While Theorem 2 claims that the DF model can represent the cycle structure when d>=3, the proof only shows that it cannot represent cycles when d=2. It seems that the claims of Theorem 2 depend on Theorem 3.

Novelty

The proposed method seems novel to my knowledge for addressing ranking problems. However, I feel that the technical contribution is not enough.

As mentioned in Section 2, several existing studies have already focused on intransitivity and proposed to extend the BTL model to higher dimensions. Although the approaches are different, the concept of extending higher dimensions will somewhat overlap with that of the proposed method.

While the theoretical results show advantages against the BTL model, the results do not explain how much the proposed method essentially contributes to the problem of intransitivity. For example, the proposed method selects the element with the largest difference looks like max pooling, but it would also be possible to consider other architectures that compute probabilities using two embedding vectors, such as taking the inner product and the average. If such other simple siamese-type models do not provide the expressive power like the proposed method, it would be convincing that the novelty of founding the proposed approach is essential. More advanced theoretical results, such as sample complexity, would have also been convincing in showing the novelty and importance of the proposed method.

Minor comments and questions
- On page 2, 'approaches.The' -> 'approaches. The'?
- On page 2, I recommend using either 'Rank-centrality' or 'Rank centrality' in the paper.
- On page 3, '[10]. Previous work [4,10]' -> 'Previous work [4,10]'?
- On page 3, there is no explanation of the variables of the BCI model, such as 'i_{chest}' and 'j_{blade}.'
- On page 3, what is the precise 'LRPR'?
- On page 3, there seems to be no precise pointer to the citation for 'the context dependent salient feature model.' Is it (Bower and Balzano, 2020)?
- On page 3, 'NP-hard problem .' -> 'NP-hard problem.'?
- On page 4, the distinguishing feature model has been abbreviated as the DF model on page 1. Once a term is shortened, the abbreviation should continue to be used.
- On page 4, it seems that the sentence 'a two step procedure if followed ...' is incomplete.
- On page 6, I recommend clarifying references for used datasets and compared methods.
- On page 7, the sentence 'The basic performance ...' seems incomplete.
- On page 7, what is the precise 'RC'? It should be mentioned if it means the abbreviation of Rank Centrality.
- On page 8, why is the BTL model not contained in the compared methods?
- On page 8, 'Relu' -> 'ReLU'?
- On page 9, 'realworld' -> 'real world'?
- On page 9, 'Table 7.4' -> 'Table 1'?
- In Reference, The information of (Negahban et al., 2015) is incomplete.

References
- He et al., GNNRank: Learning Global Rankings from Pairwise Comparisons via Directed Graph Neural Networks, ICML 2022.
- Bower and Balzano, Preference Modeling with Context-Dependent Salient Features, ICML 2020.

content.title: Distinguishing Feature Model for Ranking From Pairwise Comparisons
content.abstract: We consider the problem of ranking a set of items from pairwise comparisons among them when the underlying preferences are intransitive in nature. Intransitivity is a common occurrence in real world data sets and we introduce a flexible and natural parametric model for pairwise comparisons that we call the \emph{Distinguishing Feature Model} (DF) to capture this. Under this model, the items have an unknown but fixed embedding and the pairwise comparison between a pair of items depends probabilisitically on the feature in the embedding that can best distinguish the items. We study several theoretical properties including how it generalizes the popular transitive Bradley-Terry-Luce model. With just an embedding dimension  $d = 3$, we show that the proposed model can capture  arbitrarily long cyclic dependencies. Furthermore, we explicitly show the type of preference relations that cannot be modelled under the DF model for $d=3$. On the algorithmic side, we propose a Siamese type neural network based algorithm which can learn to predict well under the DF model while at the same time being interpretable in the sense that the embeddings learnt can be extracted directly from the learnt model. Our experimental results show that the model outperforms  standard baselines in both synthetic and real world ranking datasets.
